coverage: Nine stories · Space data centers, 1Password breach, Ladybird browser, chatbot data, AI toys, Waymo, Neuralink, WhatsApp, asteroid crater

cards.headline: FCC approves SpaceX plan for up to 1 million data-center satellites
cards.summary: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which regulates US airwaves, gave SpaceX conditional approval for Starmind, up to 1 million solar-powered satellites meant to process AI data in orbit and relay results to Earth through Starlink. Ars Technica says that would raise the number of satellites in orbit about 50-fold. Astronomers warn the bright satellites would hurt night-sky observation, and it is still unclear whether space data centers can work at scale.
cards.whyItMatters: AI needs huge amounts of computing power and electricity. Where we put data centers, on Earth or in orbit, affects energy, the environment and the view of the night sky.

csp.connection: Data centers are large groups of networked computers; Starmind would link them to Earth through other satellites.

cards.headline: 1Password breach exposes customer names and emails, not passwords
cards.summary: Password manager 1Password says an attacker took over an employee's GitHub account, used it to push malicious code to backend servers, and copied names and email addresses from a subset of customers. The company says saved passwords stayed safe because vaults are encrypted with keys only users hold. It lengthened emailed sign-in codes from six digits to ten letters and numbers to make guessing harder.
cards.whyItMatters: Stolen emails can be used for phishing, fake messages that trick you into giving up logins. Encryption kept the most sensitive data safe even after the servers were breached.

csp.connection: Longer codes with more possible characters make brute-force guessing take far longer.

cards.headline: Ladybird, a browser built from scratch, releases its first download
cards.summary: Almost every web browser runs on one of three engines, the code that turns web pages into what you see: Chrome's Blink, Safari's WebKit or Firefox's Gecko. Ladybird, a nonprofit project, wrote its own engine from scratch and released its first downloadable alpha, an early test version, for Mac and Linux. An Ars Technica reviewer found it handled Google Maps and YouTube well, but its creators warn it is not yet secure.
cards.whyItMatters: When most browsers share one engine, websites get built for that engine instead of open web standards. A new engine helps reveal where sites break those shared rules.

csp.connection: Alpha releases let users find bugs early, part of the iterative testing cycle in software development.

cards.headline: 42 states try to stop Character.AI from selling users' chats
cards.summary: Character.AI, an app for chatting with AI characters, filed for bankruptcy in October. A group of 42 state attorneys general says it plans to auction chat histories from more than 21 million US accounts, including more than 2.1 million registered to minors. They say a buyer would not have to follow the old privacy policy, let users delete their data, or limit how the data is used.
cards.whyItMatters: Conversations with chatbots can be very personal. When an app shuts down or is sold, the data you shared may outlive the app itself.

csp.connection: Stored data can be copied, sold and reused long after it was collected, beyond what users expected.

cards.headline: New York bans AI chatbot toys for five years
cards.summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a five-year ban on selling toys, such as dolls and robots, that use the internet to hold AI conversations with children. Her office cited a consumer group's tests that found some toys discussed inappropriate topics, had few parental controls and grew less safe the longer they talked. Some could record a child's voice or scan their face. Violators face fines of up to $15,000 per day.
cards.whyItMatters: AI chatbots can say unexpected things, and toys may collect kids' voices and faces. Lawmakers are deciding where AI products are allowed.

csp.connection: AI chatbots generate responses instead of following a fixed script, so their output is hard to fully predict or test.

cards.headline: Waymo robotaxis pulled off freeways after construction-zone mistakes
cards.summary: California's Department of Motor Vehicles banned Waymo's driverless cars from state freeways after they repeatedly drove into closed construction zones, and one tried to pass highway patrol cars slowing traffic. Waymo paused freeway rides in all its markets. Waymo says no one was hurt. A Carnegie Mellon safety expert told The Verge that earlier software fixes did not solve the problem.
cards.whyItMatters: Self-driving cars must handle rare situations, like temporary lane closures. Software that works in cities can still fail on unusual roads.

csp.connection: Programs must handle edge cases; a fix that passes some tests may still fail in new situations.

cards.headline: Neuralink gets FDA go-ahead for a larger brain-implant trial
cards.summary: Neuralink says the US Food and Drug Administration approved a "pivotal" trial, a larger, later-stage study, of its brain-computer interface for people with ALS, a disease that weakens muscle control. The implant reads brain signals tied to movement, and software turns them into commands to control a computer. Neuralink says 30+ people have used it so far. The trial will test usefulness and long-term safety.
cards.whyItMatters: Brain-computer interfaces could help people who cannot move or speak use phones and computers. Careful trials test whether they are safe before wider use.

csp.connection: Software must find patterns in noisy brain-signal data and translate them into specific commands.

cards.headline: WhatsApp adds scheduled messages, up to two weeks ahead
cards.summary: WhatsApp is rolling out scheduled messages worldwide over the coming weeks. You hold the send button, pick a time from 10 minutes to 14 days away, and the message arrives looking like any other. It works for texts, photos and videos in one-on-one and group chats. WhatsApp says scheduled messages are still end-to-end encrypted, and will arrive on time even if your phone is off.
cards.whyItMatters: You can wish a friend luck right before a test or say happy birthday at midnight in their time zone. It also shows how apps handle timing behind the scenes.

csp.connection: Scheduling is event-driven programming: code runs when a condition, like a set time, is reached.

cards.headline: Spacecraft finds stadium-sized crater from NASA's asteroid crash test
cards.summary: In 2022, NASA crashed its DART spacecraft into the asteroid Dimorphos to test whether we could push an asteroid off course. Europe's Hera spacecraft has now arrived and found a crater about the size of a stadium, nearly as wide as the 151-meter asteroid. Dimorphos is now tumbling, and hundreds of boulders orbit the asteroid pair. Hera will soon move closer and release two small satellites.
cards.whyItMatters: Asteroids that could hit Earth come in many shapes and materials. Measurements from Hera will improve the computer models scientists use to plan future deflections.

csp.connection: Real measurements are used to check and improve computer simulations of how asteroids respond to impacts.
